newsitem.title: UK: Dry weather draws mice, weeds to UK sugar beet crop.
newsitem.headline: Dry weather draws mice, weeds to UK sugar beet crop.

text.p: Lack of rainfall over Britain's beet growing areas is starting to take its toll on the 1997/98 crop as weeds and mice take advantage of the dry conditions, beets experts said on Wednesday.
Rain would be needed in May to ensure stable germination and avoid losing the head start given by early sowings, they said.
While farmers managed to sow into fairly moist beds in some areas such as the west Midlands, northern areas had dry and potentially damaging weather.
"In the north, in the York area, it's very dry indeed. As soon as the soil was turned it seemed to dry out very quickly," said an official at the National Farmers Union (NFU).

Problems had been reported of mice attacking seeds lying on dry ground, she said. Weeds, which can stunt beet growth, are another problem as the high daytime temperatures have prevented the application of herbicide.
High temperatures can also lead to an increased risk of aphids, which can feed as soon as the beet leaf emerges, leading to the presence of virus yellows.
"It's patchy emergence and weeds are really coming through strong," the NFU official said.
"So it means that it's going to be quite a costly crop to grow because they (farmers) will need to spray more times than usual to get rid of the weeds."
East Anglia, Britain's major beet growing area, is also reported to be fairly dry.

In its Wednesday report, German statistician F.O. Licht said dry weather was expected to continue in western Europe's beet belt -- where drillings were mostly completed this week -- for at least another week.
"Crops are in no immediate danger from the persistent lack of rain, but more moisture will need to return in May to ensure stable germination and early development," Licht said.
British Sugar has said the crop is holding up well despite the dry conditions, as beet seeds were sown into beds which already had sufficient moisture content.
"It's fairly early days and a little early to start panicking about the crop," said a spokesman on Wednesday.

Ground drillings were 100 percent complete by April 5, ahead of last year and before the end of British Sugar's recommended drilling period, as farmers took advantage of mild spring weather to sow early.
Independent forecaster WSC said near drought to drought conditions dominate western European arable areas, including major maize areas of France.
It forecast very cool and unsettled weather in the east from Friday to Sunday and fair and seasonably cool weather in the west. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 8064
